1.pericope_label: David smites the Philistines and takes Gath, reduces Moab, defeats Hadadezer king of Zobah and the Syrians of Damascus, and brings the shields of gold and much brass to Jerusalem

schools.summary: Henry sets the campaign against the communion with God in word and prayer recorded just before, so that David goes out conquering and to conquer as Jacob lifted up his feet after his vision, and draws five observations from the sequence: that those long the enemies of the Israel of God are brought down at last, as all opposing rule and power will be put down by the Son of David; that men lose their power at the moment they think to confirm it, Hadadezer being smitten as he went to establish his dominion; that a horse is a vain thing for safety, which David both said and seems to have believed, since he houghed the chariot horses rather than trust them; that the enemies of the church are often made to ruin themselves by helping one another, the Syrians of Damascus being smitten when they came to the aid of a losing ally; and that the wealth of the sinner is sometimes found to have been laid up for the just, since as the tabernacle was built of the spoils of Egypt so the temple was built of the spoils of the nations, which he takes for a happy presage of the interest the Gentiles would have in the gospel church.

Ellicott reads the opening formula as a mere mark of transition rather than a date, since it does not put these events in direct sequence with the last chapter but has been carried over unaltered from the history both books drew on, finds a second mark of the same hand in the first verse where Samuel speaks of taking the bridle of the mother city and the chronicler writes that David took Gath and her daughter towns, rejects the apology that the massacre of the Moabites was omitted to clear David of barbarity, adding that a writer possessed with the national hatred of the aliens who had oppressed his people was not likely to judge such a slaughter by a modern standard, and is minutely textual on the campaign, that the name should be Hadadezer since Hadad was a Syrian god worshipped from the Euphrates to Edom and recognisable in Benhadad, that Zobah lay towards Hamath somewhere near Emesa, that this book thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen is likelier than the reading in Samuel because a kingdom in the great plain of Aram would be strong in both, that houghing is the cutting of the sinews of the hind legs to disable the animal, and that the hundred chariots David kept were a luxury in Israel, the stud being recruited from Egypt only in the next reign and against an express prohibition; Keil and Delitzsch give the first verse as their specimen of the chronicler habit of paraphrastic explanation, the figure of the bridle standing for the loss of hegemony and the plain words standing for the figure, and call the omission of the Moabite massacre surprising, no reason for it being discoverable, refusing the same apology on the ground that he does not pass over the like treatment of the captives at Rabbah later in the same book.

debates.question: Why does the chronicler omit the massacre of the Moabite captives?

sides.position: not to clear David of barbarity, since the same writer records the like treatment of the captives at Rabbah; no reason for the omission is discoverable
not from any modern scruple, since a writer filled with the national hatred of those aliens would not have judged the slaughter as we do

debates.question: Which reading of the cavalry numbers is right?

sides.position: this book thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen, since a kingdom of the great plain would be strong in chariots and horses

outliers: Keil and Delitzsch alone treat the chapter as evidence about the chronicler method rather than about David, reading the first verse as a specimen of paraphrase and the omissions as a problem of sources.
Henry alone reads the campaign devotionally, taking the conquests as the fruit of the communion with God recorded in the chapter before.
themes: a formula of transition mistaken for a date
a figure of speech turned into plain geography
spoils carried from the nations to the temple
a massacre passed over without explanation

9.pericope_label: Tou king of Hamath sends Hadoram with vessels of silver, gold and brass, which David dedicates to the LORD with the spoil of the nations; Abishai smites eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt and garrisons are set in Edom

schools.summary: Henry takes the presents and the preservation as the lessons of the passage, that it is our interest to make friends of those who have the presence of God with them, which is what the king of Hamath did in courting the favour of a conqueror, and that since it is vain to contend with the Son of David the presents we bring him are not vessels of silver and gold but our hearts and ourselves as living sacrifices; what God blesses us with we must honour him with, which is why the gifts of friends and the spoils of enemies went alike into the store for building the temple, that being most truly our own which has been consecrated to the Lord; he fastens on the repeated clause that the Lord preserved David whithersoever he went and answers it with the remark that those are always under the eye of God who have God always in their eye, and reads the record of judgment and justice as showing why the power was given, not that a man may look great with it but that he may do good with it.

Clarke notes that the king called Tou here is Toi in the older book, and resolves the difficulty about the Edomite victory by the law of agency, that a battle won by the general David sent is with propriety ascribed to the commander-in-chief who sent him.

Ellicott explains the variation in the king name by the two Hebrew letters constantly confused in manuscripts, decides for the form used here, reports that the versions wander much further, the Syriac making the man a king of the Antiochenes and the Arabic a king of Antioch by apparent confusion with an Assyrian name, and that a scholar of his own day believed he had read the name on the stones from Hamath newly brought to the British Museum; on the envoy he allows that the form here looks right while the Joram of Samuel may be correct, since an inscription of Sargon calls a Hamathite king by a name compounded with that of the God of Israel, who was evidently not unknown there; he glosses the errand as blessing, that is pronouncing the victor happy, notes that the clause about the long war with Hadadezer is curtailed, that where Samuel says David dedicated the spoil this book says he brought it so as to avoid a tautology, that the nations named should include Edom rather than Aram as all the versions support, and that the mention of Amalek refers either to the old raid or more probably to a campaign nowhere recorded; from a comparison of the three accounts of the Edomite war he infers that Edom invaded Judah while David was occupied in the north and that a column was detached southward to meet it, and he observes that the six peoples reduced here had all been enemies of David ill-fated predecessor.

debates.question: Whose victory was the slaughter in the Valley of Salt?

sides.position: Abishai won it, and the older book credits David because a victory won by the general he sent is properly ascribed to the commander-in-chief
the accounts differ further than that, and read together they show Edom invading Judah in David absence and a column detached southward under his captains

debates.question: Which king of Hamath, and which envoy?

sides.position: Tou here against Toi in Samuel, the Hebrew letters for w and y being constantly confused, with the form used here correct
the envoy form here looks right, but the Joram of Samuel may stand, since an Assyrian inscription shows the God of Israel was known at Hamath

outliers: Ellicott alone brings an Assyrian royal inscription and a newly read Hamathite stone to bear on two proper names in the verse.
Henry alone turns the tribute into a lesson about what may be brought to the Son of David, who takes hearts where he is offered vessels.
themes: a rival king who chose friendship
tribute laid up for a temple

14.pericope_label: David reigned over all Israel executing judgment and justice, and these were his officers, Joab over the host, Jehoshaphat the recorder, Zadok and Abimelech the priests, Shavsha the scribe, Benaiah over the Cherethites and Pelethites, and the sons of David chief about the king

schools.summary: Clarke gives the plain equivalents of the titles, the man over the host being general-in-chief and the recorder the king remembrancer or historiographer royal, states the traditional solution of the double priesthood, that Zadok and the other named man were both high priests serving at Gibeon and at Jerusalem, notes that the scribe called Shavsha here appears in Samuel as Seraiah, and reports the fuller rabbinic tradition about the captain of the guard, that he presided over both the greater and the lesser council and consulted the sacred lots, and that at his word the archers and slingers went out to battle, the sons of David being highest in authority.

Ellicott takes the verb of the first verse as describing a permanent state of things rather than a single act and distinguishes the pair of words that follow, the first naming the quality and the second the conduct which embodies it, traces the title of recorder back to its root, remembrancer, and reports that the Greek and Latin make him keeper or writer of memoranda where the eastern versions of the older book make him a leader or director; on the priests he corrects the spelling to Ahimelech son of Abiathar, sets out the difficulty that elsewhere Zadok and Abiathar are the priests of the reign and that Abiathar was himself a son of the Ahimelech whom Saul killed at Nob, and then declines the obvious remedy of reversing the names, because an Ahimelech son of Abiathar is named three separate times later in the same book and may have been acting for his father when so brief a list was drawn up, so that in the absence of further detail it would be arbitrary to alter the text of four passages at once; he identifies the two companies of the guard as the royal body-guard, an office for which eastern kings have always employed foreign mercenaries, notes that Josephus calls them exactly that, and argues from the tribal form of both names and the company they keep elsewhere with the Philistines that the guard was recruited from two Philistine tribes; on the last title he doubts the common explanation that the word simply means a secular minister, since under the monarchy the priesthood was drawn close to the crown by its judicial duties and a royal sanctuary chief priest became a great officer of state, a post worth filling with princes of the blood, so that the chronicler writing later has replaced a term which would by then have given offence; Keil and Delitzsch agree independently that the phrase is a paraphrase, listing this very verse beside the first as a specimen of the chronicler habit of explaining an older expression.

debates.question: Should the names of the priests be reversed to Abiathar son of Ahimelech?

sides.position: no; an Ahimelech son of Abiathar is named three times later in the book and may have acted for his father, so altering four passages would be arbitrary
the question does not arise, since both men were high priests at once, one at Gibeon and one at Jerusalem

debates.question: What does it mean that the sons of David were chief about the king?

sides.position: the older book calls them priests, and this book substitutes a phrase that would not offend a later age; the word is not merely secular, since a royal sanctuary chief priest was a great officer of state
it is one of the chronicler paraphrastic explanations, of a piece with his handling of the bridle in the first verse
simply that they were highest in authority

outliers: Ellicott alone refuses an easy emendation of the priestly names on the ground that it would require altering four separate passages.
Clarke alone preserves the rabbinic tradition that the captain of the guard sat in both councils and consulted the sacred lots.
themes: a reign described as a settled state
titles translated out of an older court
a knot in the priestly names left untied
a foreign guard around an Israelite king
